query: For multi-component concentrated alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their strength and deformation or failure behavior, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the conditions over which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multi‐component concentrated alloys, increasing the degree of short-range order (SRO) via controlled heat treatments enhances local fluctuations in planar fault energies, which serve as pinning sites for dislocations. This results in higher yield strength and altered deformation mechanisms—specifically more planar slip and localized strain—compared to alloys with lower SRO.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-component concentrated alloy (e.g., CrCoNi or similar FCC MCCA) in a homogenized, as-processed state with a relatively random atomic distribution.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat treatment regimen designed to tune the degree of SRO without changing the overall alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Tensile deformation under room-temperature conditions in FCC structured samples with similar grain textures, ensuring that the only variable is the SRO level.
generation.structural_mediator: The local degree of short-range order (SRO) that modulates the distribution of planar fault energies.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced SRO leads to increased fluctuations in local planar fault energies, creating hard atomic motifs that pin dislocation motion. This pinning forces dislocations to follow more planar slip paths and promotes strain localization, thereby increasing yield strength and altering deformation behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with high SRO induced by heat treatment will exhibit significantly higher yield strength, more pronounced planar slip, and increased localization of plastic strain compared to the baseline homogenized samples with lower SRO.
generation.baseline: The homogenized alloy state with minimal SRO (i.e., a nearly random solid solution).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under tensile loading conditions in FCC multi-component concentrated alloys processed at temperatures where SRO can be thermally modulated without inducing phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative effect on yield strength and the degree of strain localization may vary with processing parameters and grain orientation. Also, contributions from other microstructural features such as grain boundaries may not be fully isolated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical alloy samples. One set receives a heat treatment intended to maximize SRO, while the other serves as an untreated baseline with minimal SRO. Characterize the SRO levels using atom probe tomography or electron nanodiffraction, then perform in situ TEM tensile tests and macroscopic tensile tests to capture dislocation dynamics, the distribution of planar fault energies, yield strength, and strain localization patterns.
measurements: Quantified SRO levels through atomistic or diffraction techniques
Dislocation slip configurations and pinning behavior (via TEM)
Yield strength and macroscopic strain localization metrics from tensile tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with enhanced SRO do not show statistically significant increases in yield strength and altered (more planar) dislocation slip mechanisms along with observable increases in local planar fault energy fluctuations compared to the baseline samples, the hypothesis that SRO governs strength through these mechanisms would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: SignificanceComplex concentrated alloys (CCAs) with multi elements in equiatomic ratios are exotic alloys but what governs their strength is currently not clearly understood. This work has proven the prime origin of strength in CCAs as arising from the fluctuations (not the averaged value) of the shear-fault energy, which is an important feature of CCAs unrecognized beforehand. Through identification of the local hard atomic motifs far beyond the traditional concept of the globally averaged short-range ordering parameters, this work has unfolded the physical basis of strength in CCAs and provides important clues for designing high-strength CCAs by focusing on the alloy composition to produce large fault-energy fluctuations. Local chemical short-range ordering (SRO) and spatial fluctuations of planar fault energy are important features of multi-element and metastable complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). Arising from them, dislocations in such alloys are distinctively wavy in both static and migrating conditions; yet, such effects on strength have remained unknown. Hybrid MC/MD simulations have proven to be a powerful tool to explore the effects of atomic segregation and SRO on the mechanical properties of MEAs and HEAs. For example, Jian et al. used hybrid MC and MD simulations to investigate the role of lattice distortion (LD) and SRO on the formation and evolution of dislocations in a CoCrNi MEA. These simulations suggested that yield strength was controlled by the strain required to nucleate Shockley partial dislocations; LD lowered this strain, while SRO increased it. The hybrid MC/MD simulations of Li et al. demonstrated that increasing SRO in the CoCrNi MEA increased the ruggedness of the energy landscape, thereby raising barriers to dislocation activity and increasing strength. Short-range ordering in HEAs is more complex than that of MEAs (with the increased number of distinct atomic pairs in HEAs), suggesting that HEAs provide a richer environment for tailoring their orders and microstructures to achieve superior strength and ductility. Is it possible to introduce SRO in HEAs to enhance both strength and ductility? If so, what microstructures are required? And, what is the underlying mechanistic reason for these increases? The exceptional mechanical strength of medium/high-entropy alloys has been attributed to hardening in random solid solutions. Here, we evidence non-random chemical mixing in a CrCoNi alloy, resulting from short-range ordering. A data-mining approach of electron nanodiffraction enabled the study, which is assisted by neutron scattering, atom probe tomography, and diffraction simulation using first-principles theory models. Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11). The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior. These findings uncover short-range order and the resulted chemical heterogeneities behind the mechanical strength in CrCoNi, providing general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys for the design of strong and ductile materials. decision.trend: Starting around 2018, efforts to understand mechanical behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys (MCCAs) focused first on compiling property databases (PMC6290247) and documenting the role of metastability and twinning in FCC high-entropy alloys (PMC6006257). Subsequent atomistic simulations of CoCrFeMnNi (PMC7801446) showcased partial dislocations nucleating from grain boundaries, highlighting the importance of local structure. Studies of refractory HEAs revealed an unexpected role of edge dislocations in controlling strength (PMC8446014). More recently, short-range chemical ordering (SRO) has emerged as a key mechanism that influences local stacking-fault energies, dislocation slip behaviors, and, ultimately, alloy strength (PMC9636235, PMC9645729). The latest findings show that strength in metastable complex concentrated alloys can be dominated by local fluctuations in shear-fault energy rather than just global averages (PMC10041143). Nevertheless, a unifying testable explanation for precisely how composition and microstructure (including SRO and dislocation modes) govern deformation and failure has remained elusive.
decision.unsolved: Although these works collectively point to SRO-driven changes in fault energies and dislocation behavior as critical in determining strength and ductility of MCCAs, definitive, direct evidence linking local chemical Order–dislocation interactions to macroscopic properties is still missing. Specifically, a controlled and quantitative demonstration has yet to show how variations in local atomic configurations (short-range order versus relative disorder) alter slip mechanisms, dislocation paths, and the resulting strain hardening unambiguously.
decision.lever: Conduct a heat-treatment–based controlled-variable experiment to tune the degree of short-range ordering in a single MCCA composition, followed by in situ diffraction/TEM mechanical tests and atomistic simulations to correlate the measured SRO distribution with dislocation slip paths and fault energies.
decision.why: The literature increasingly identifies local short-range ordering and associated planar-fault-energy fluctuations as a potentially decisive factor governing strength. Directly manipulating SRO by adjusting thermal histories (without changing overall composition) and linking the resulting microstructure to in situ mechanical response would rigorously test the hypothesis that local fault-energy variations dominate dislocation activity. Detecting statistically meaningful differences in dislocation configurations, slip planarity, and mechanical properties among different SRO states would confirm that local chemical fluctuations dictate strength; a null result (no difference) would falsify it.
